body:
Turn arithmetic into a timed experiment

An arithmetic identity tells us what the computer should do, but not where its qubits should live or which operations can run together. The compiler must turn that identity into a legal sequence of measurements while preserving both output values and relative phases.

Section VIII follows this conversion. It assigns logical registers to code blocks, schedules measurements and corrections, and tracks when factories can supply another resource state. The architecture then implements those logical instructions through physical gates and ion transport.

Arithmetic

The arithmetic specifies the reversible map and its Toffoli consumption.

Schedule

The schedule determines which operations overlap and how many measurement layers remain.

Device

The block and factory allocation determines how many physical qubits the schedule requires.

Keep the interface fixed; change the implementation

The compiler separates a component's specification from its implementation. A spec declares the map; a def supplies smaller operations that realize it. For an n-bit adder with \(a\) clean work qubits, \[U_{\rm add}|x,y\rangle=|x,x+y\bmod 2^n\rangle,\qquad V_{\rm def}|x,y,0^a\rangle=(U_{\rm add}|x,y\rangle)|0^a\rangle.\]

The second equation includes the cleanup promise: every working qubit returns to zero. A measurement-based implementation satisfies it after its outcome-dependent corrections. Ripple carry and carry lookahead can implement the same map while requiring different placements, workspace, and time.

The contract exposes what matters

For an adder, the caller needs a correct sum and clean workspace. The implementation can choose how to achieve that contract.

Visible to the callerChosen by the implementation
Input and output registers; arithmetic modulusCarry workspace; gate decomposition; qubit placement
Correct amplitudes and phases; clean work on returnMeasurement outcomes and their correction records

Structure carries scheduling information

Keeping the hierarchy exposes useful register lifetimes. A point addition contains lookups, differences, division, square subtraction, and multiplication. Once division finishes, its history storage can serve the next adder. The compiler uses these boundaries when selecting implementations, then lowers each leaf to an instruction supported by the architecture.

A frame update changes the next measurement

Many of those instructions are Pauli measurements and classically tracked Clifford operations. If \(m\) is a Pauli readout, its projector and its relation to a Clifford \(C\) are \[\Pi_m(P)=\frac{I+(-1)^mP}{2},\qquad \Pi_m(P)C=C\Pi_m(C^\dagger PC).\] This identity lets the compiler replace an applied Clifford by a change to the observable measured later.

For example, moving a target-Z measurement through a CNOT changes it to ZZ on control and target. The software can track this change, but the resulting two-qubit support must still be measurable on the device. Accumulated Clifford frames therefore create a physical accessibility problem that the architecture must periodically clear.

What “end-to-end” includes

The paper compiles major components separately and joins their layouts through an authored routing sequence, charging 20 additional layers per point-addition window. This gives the composed schedule used in the estimate. Appendix D explains the lowering machinery, and the lookup lesson follows one important component through its scheduling choices.

title: VIII · From arithmetic to executable measurements

body:
A layer must pass two tests

Suppose two measurements act on unrelated logical values. They may be independent in the algorithm and still compete for the same physical measurement resources. Scheduling must check both the order of the computation and the capacity of the machine.

The target has 69 Q102 memory blocks, each encoding 22 logical qubits in 102 data ions. Cat-state ancillas perform Pauli measurements, and prepared CCZ states supply Toffoli operations. The table gives the per-layer limits that every placement must respect.

ResourceLimitWhat the count omits
Logical measurements per block3Pauli-support and frame compatibility
Memory-side cat-bundle pairs24 totalWhich blocks each bundle must touch
CCZ injection1Factory readiness and subsequent cleanup

If operation \(j\) depends strictly on operation \(i\), their layer numbers must satisfy \(\ell_j>\ell_i\). Removing that dependency is only the first test. The measurements must also have compatible physical supports and available ancillas in their proposed layer.

Earlier measurement, changed observable

A measurement can sometimes move earlier by changing what is measured. For Hermitian Pauli \(P\), \(\Pi_m(P)\) projects onto eigenvalue \((-1)^m\). Commuting it through Clifford \(C\) gives the identity below, illustrated by a CNOT with control \(c\) and target \(t\).

\[\Pi_m(P)C=C\Pi_m(C^\dagger PC),\qquad C^\dagger Z_tC=Z_cZ_t\quad(C=\mathrm{CNOT}).\]

The transformed observable can involve more qubits than the original one. The scheduler must therefore test its new support at every candidate position, rather than assuming that algebraic commutation guarantees a legal physical measurement.

A missing sign can wait

A pending correction need not delay a measurement when it changes only the sign assigned to the result.

\[\Pi_m(Z)X^s=X^s\Pi_{m\oplus s}(Z).\]

An unresolved Pauli correction changes only the interpretation of a result. In the identity above, measure Z now and record its logical outcome as the raw bit XOR \(s\). The scheduler stores this expression until \(s\) becomes known.

A missing basis cannot wait

The situation changes when a pending correction determines which basis must be measured. The following cases separate a delayed sign from a delayed basis.

Pending correctionRequired observableConsequence
\(X^s\)\((-1)^sZ\)Same measurement; interpret its sign later
\(H^s\)Z if \(s=0\); X if \(s=1\)Basis changes; wait for \(s\)

An unresolved Clifford can instead change the measurement basis, as the example shows. That measurement must wait for the controlling result. An earlier anticommuting measurement also blocks motion, because exchanging X and Z readouts changes the experiment.

Algorithm 1: scan backward, stop at a real obstacle

Algorithm 1 begins at a serially valid position and scans backward. It conjugates the observable through Clifford updates, revises outcome expressions, and tests the candidate layers. It stops at a causal obstacle or dependency and commits the earliest legal placement found. The resulting depth comes from this greedy legal schedule.

Two different reasons to stall

A stall can come from either shared equipment or unresolved information. These two examples isolate the causes.

Resource stall

Even independent CCZ injections use separate layers because they share the single injection interface.

Basis stall

A measurement with an unresolved basis waits for its controlling bit even when a physical port is idle.

Commutation becomes a parity test

The compiler performs its commutation tests using binary Pauli masks. Ignoring overall phase, write \(P(x,z)=X^xZ^z\). The parity in the following identity determines whether two Paulis commute: \[P(x,z)P(x',z')=(-1)^{x\cdot z'+z\cdot x'}P(x',z')P(x,z).\]

For instance, \(X_1X_2\) commutes with \(Z_1Z_2\) because two local anticommutations cancel, whereas \(X_1\) anticommutes with that pair. Block-local masks make this test inexpensive across the full instruction stream; support and resource checks still determine whether commuting operations fit together.
summary: Moving a measurement earlier requires both causal permission and physical capacity. A pending sign can be tracked; a pending basis can force a wait.
title: IX · Scheduling with Pauli frames and finite resources

body:
Arrange qubits so corrections stay local

A ripple-carry adder passes information from one bit to the next. We can exploit that motion by placing each pair of operand bits beside its carry workspace. In Q102, which encodes 22 logical qubits per block, this makes most of the adder's corrections local.

Place seven triples \((x_i,y_i,c_i)\) in each block and use the remaining slot as a carry relay. Thirty-seven blocks form the 256-bit lane. Most CNOT and CZ operations then remain within a block and enter its tracked Clifford frame; only the carry crossing a block boundary needs a relay.

The placement matches the serial computation: while the carry advances, completed parts of the lane can release or rearrange their workspace. This is the opportunity for hiding routing time.

A move is a parity measurement plus cleanup

To move an unknown logical state, first create an entangled copy through a parity measurement, then erase the source with its phase correction. The table follows that state transfer.

Operation and correctionState after correction
Start\((\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle)_s|+\rangle_d\)
Measure \(Z_sZ_d\to a\); apply \(X_d^a\)\(\alpha|00\rangle+\beta|11\rangle\)
Measure \(X_s\to b\); apply \(Z_d^b\)\((\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle)_d\)

The copy stage in the diagram spreads one state's computational-basis information into an entangled pair. Measuring the source then leaves the state at the destination. The readout determines a phase correction that can be tracked classically.

Distribute a control; erase by parity

To distribute a control farther, prepare Bell links in one XX-measurement layer and join them to the source in a ZZ layer. After corrections, the result is \(\alpha|0\cdots0\rangle+\beta|1\cdots1\rangle\). X-measuring the spare copies returns the control to one qubit with a Z correction given by the parity of their readouts.

The receiving pairs shown here have offsets \(s_1\) and \(s_1\oplus s_2\), removed by the displayed X corrections. The two-layer construction needs suitable placement and cat resources. With spare positions, two such moves can also exchange remote values in parallel.

Figure 2 shows the generic remote-gate gadget. The tailored adder placement reduces how often that gadget must be repeated: most arithmetic CNOT and CZ operations already act within one encoded block.

Use the disappearing carry as a routing opportunity

A sum overflowing a 256-bit register needs a short correction at the bottom. That correction can use workspace already released by the main carry sweep.

\[p=2^{256}-c,\quad c=2^{32}+977,\qquad x+y=s+q2^{256}\equiv s+qc\pmod p.\]

A modular addition illustrates how routing overlaps useful work. After the full 256-bit sum, overflow requires a 65-bit correction by \(c\), followed by a high-32-bit phase comparator. The displayed field identity explains the correction; Appendix B accounts for its truncated carries and boundary cases.

Full carry-out addition

As the reverse carry sweep finishes a block, release its work slots immediately. The next operation can begin using those positions before the entire lane is cleared.

Small correction

Park the low source bits, distribute the overflow control, and load the short constant \(qc\) into the released workspace. The 65-bit correction adder can now use the same local arrangement.

Close the layout

Afterward, erase the loaded constant, restore the parked source, and repair the measurement phases. Those cleanup operations overlap the parts of the carry schedule that do not depend on them.

Routing almost disappears from the serial path

We can now compare the serial arithmetic with the routed component. The remaining difference measures how much movement failed to overlap useful work.

\[\underbrace{510}_{\text{full adder}}+\underbrace{128}_{\text{small adder}}+\underbrace{31}_{\text{unhidden comparison}}=669,\qquad D_{\rm compiled}=674.\]

The serial arithmetic subtotal is 669 layers; the compiled component uses 674. The five additional layers fit within the separately charged CliNR seam delay of about 7.73 layers, so charging both would count the same wait twice. Up to three compatible measurements per block enable the rearrangement behind the carry sweep.

The same rule governs the whole window

The same principle shapes the other components. Zipper lookup overlaps two traversals, shrinking gcd values release history storage, and square-product shifts also align registers. The peak is 68 active blocks plus the index block. Appendix C returns the whole window to its entry placement, with a 20-layer composition allowance.
summary: Place operand bits and carries together, then rearrange completed regions behind the carry sweep. Movement can overlap the arithmetic it supports.
title: X · Moving data while arithmetic is already running

body:
Correct arithmetic and executable scheduling are separate claims

A circuit can return every tested integer correctly and still have a wrong quantum phase. It can also represent the correct quantum operation while asking the hardware to perform incompatible measurements. Verification must address these two failure modes separately.

The semantic checker compares the quantum map and its workspace promises. The schedule checker tests dependencies, supports, and resources such as cat bundles. Neither check substitutes for the other, so the paper organizes evidence around both.

Choose a contract that sees the possible bug

The contract must record whatever a possible bug could change. The table compares value-only, phase-sensitive, and full-operator descriptions.

ContractWhat it recordsTypical use
Basis\(|x\rangle\mapsto|f(x)\rangle\)Reversible arithmetic labels
Basis plus phase\(|x\rangle\mapsto e^{i\theta(x)}|f(x)\rangle\)Phase-aware arithmetic and cleanup
Full operatorGeneral quantum evolution, including corrected measurement branchesSmall quantum primitives

For example, identity and Z leave the same computational-basis labels unchanged, but act differently on \(|+\rangle\). A value-only test cannot distinguish them. The contract must include phase whenever phase can affect the caller.

Erasing a work bit leaves a visible phase

A temporary AND gives a direct phase test: compute it, X-measure its ancilla, and follow the sign left on the controls.

\[\sum_{a,b}\alpha_{ab}|a,b,0\rangle\xrightarrow{\text{compute AND}}\sum_{a,b}\alpha_{ab}|a,b,ab\rangle\xrightarrow{M_X\to m}\sum_{a,b}\alpha_{ab}(-1)^{mab}|a,b\rangle.\]

The displayed AND example conditions on an X-readout result \(m\). Its remaining state has the sign \((-1)^{mab}\). Applying \(\mathrm{CZ}^m\) cancels that sign and recovers the intended coherent state.

CaseMeasurement phaseCorrectionNet phase
\(mab=0\)\(+1\)\(+1\)\(+1\)
\(m=a=b=1\)\(-1\)\(-1\)\(+1\)

The drawing uses a transparent compute-AND operation so the cleanup can be checked directly. An optimized magic-state implementation may realize that computation differently, but it must preserve the same corrected map.

Prove the parent from its children

Once the children are verified, compose their maps and check the workspace at the parent boundary. This is the equality the parent must satisfy.

\[V_r\cdots V_1|x\rangle|0\rangle_A=(U_{\rm spec}|x\rangle)|0\rangle_A.\]

A parent component is verified by composing its child contracts. In the equation, \(V_i\) are the children, \(U_{\rm spec}\) the required parent operation, and \(A\) its workspace. The checker binds their registers, checks input domains, and verifies every claimed clean output. Composition establishes the parent on the domains where those child contracts hold.

Testing cannot certify rare approximation failures

The paper also tests the approximate secp256k1 adder on 100,000 reproducibly sampled pairs and tests other widths. A bug occurring with probability \(\varepsilon\) under that distribution escapes \(N\) independent tests with probability \((1-\varepsilon)^N\). The separate approximation bounds in Section IV and Appendix B address the rare specified failure events.

Check the failure mode with the right experiment

Different checks target different faults. The following table connects each reported experiment to the kind of mistake it can expose.

Reported checkWhat it can catch
Basis simulation of the 674-layer adderWrong arithmetic
Reduced-scale phase-aware and superposition testsWrong relative phases
Cat, injection, block, and routing validationIllegal parallelism or unavailable resources
Analytic cost envelopes and small full programsMissing work and composition errors

What remains necessary for independent reproduction

Independent reproduction needs the parameters, architecture, layouts, code versions, saved schedule, metrics, and check results. The paper describes retained artifacts, but its prose does not supply the executable component library. This website checks the exposed identities and examples; it has not rerun the authors' internal compiler or noise simulations.
summary: Check the coherent map and the physical schedule separately. Correct integers can hide a phase error, and correct gates can exceed available measurement resources.
title: XI · What the compiler checks, and what those checks prove

body:
Follow the register's meaning as well as its location

Follow one point addition through the machine, keeping track of both the meaning and location of each register. Here the two inputs are \(P,Q\), their sum is \(R\), and all coordinate arithmetic is modulo \(p=2^{256}-2^{32}-977\) on the nonexceptional branch.

Figure 21 begins with packed coordinates, opens an interleaved arithmetic lane, and returns the result to the original arrangement. A spent value can release its qubits before its measurement phase is repaired. This separation allows useful work and routing to overlap.

Two identities drive register reuse

Write the points as \((x_P,y_P)\) and \((x_Q,y_Q)\). Form differences \(d_x=x_P-x_Q\), \(d_y=y_P-y_Q\), then the slope \(\lambda=d_y/d_x\). The affine result is \[x_R=\lambda^2-x_P-x_Q,\qquad y_R=\lambda(x_P-x_R)-y_P.\]

We do not need to store every quantity in those formulas separately. Rearranging them gives \[d_x+3x_Q-\lambda^2=x_Q-x_R,\qquad\lambda(x_Q-x_R)=y_R+y_Q.\] These identities explain why the first register can become \(x_Q-x_R\), while the slope register becomes \(y_R+y_Q\).

The register trace

The same two registers change meaning as the addition proceeds. Reading the table from top to bottom follows those meanings before adding their physical locations.

StageFirst coordinate registerSecond coordinate register
Differences\(d_x\)\(d_y\)
Division\(d_x\)\(\lambda\)
Add \(3x_Q\), subtract square\(x_Q-x_R\)\(\lambda\)
Multiply\(x_Q-x_R\)\(y_R+y_Q\)
Remove offsets; negate first\(x_R\)\(y_R\)

1. Lookup, subtract, release

First keep the 16-bit index live and load a table coordinate beside its accumulator coordinate. Subtract to form the difference, then X-measure the spent table value. Its positions become workspace while its readout mask records a later phase correction. Independent x and y work can overlap where their dependencies allow.

2. Divide while the workspace changes shape

Next place the binary-gcd values in the U/V lane. Their shrinking high bits make room for compressed history and the other operand. Replay turns \(d_y\) into the slope, then clears the record. The largest simultaneous allocation is 68 active blocks plus the index block.

3. Compute the new x coordinate indirectly

Load \(3x_Q\), add it to \(d_x\), then subtract \(\lambda^2\). The register now contains \(x_Q-x_R\). Product shifts also supply useful alignment. Algorithm 6 adds and removes a random field mask around this sequence so the square-subtraction failure analysis has a uniform target.

4. Reuse the large workspace for multiplication

Pack the inactive value and place the multiplication operands in the lane. Multiplication turns \(\lambda\) into \(y_R+y_Q\); reversing the gcd representation clears its workspace. The same region has now served both of the expensive arithmetic operations.

5. Remove offsets and accumulated lookup phases

Reload the table coordinates to remove the final offsets. Each X-cleared lookup contributes a readout mask on the same address \(j\). Repeated appearances of a coordinate word \(f(j)\) combine through \[(-1)^{m_1\cdot f(j)}(-1)^{m_2\cdot f(j)}=(-1)^{(m_1\oplus m_2)\cdot f(j)}.\]

The final phase lookup uses these combined masks and the separate mask for \(3x_Q\). Once its signs are repaired and the coordinates packed, the result occupies the same layout used at entry. The next window can therefore reuse the schedule.

Closing the layout makes component costs composable

Closing the placement loop makes separately compiled component costs composable. The paper allows 20 additional layers per window for their joins. Figure 21 supplies the logical placement sequence behind that allowance under the stated architecture model.
summary: One pair of coordinate registers changes roles throughout point addition. Its placement must return to the starting arrangement so the next window can reuse the schedule.
title: Appendix C · Follow one point-addition window through memory

body:
The run configuration is part of the result

The compiler begins with a large reversible operation and repeatedly replaces it by smaller ones. Each replacement preserves the named inputs, outputs, and clean-work promises. The process ends when every leaf can be executed by the target architecture.

Its inputs therefore include more than the arithmetic parameters: the root component, architecture, layout plan, and synthesis options all affect the result. The output is a measurement schedule and its metrics. Reproducing a layer count requires the same geometry, legal operations, concurrency, and factory recipes.

1. Lower until every leaf is legal

Consider an adder that the architecture cannot execute directly. Lowering selects a carry circuit, places its registers, and continues until each remaining operation is supported.

Choose a definition

Choose a concrete carry implementation for the abstract adder.

Bind its work

Bind its operands and temporary registers to positions in the planned code blocks.

Check each child

Retain the measurements and frame updates already supported there, and decompose the remaining operations further.

Each substitution must preserve the public map and return its promised workspace clean. Validating these substitutions composes into correctness of the root. Operations crossing blocks must also be decomposed into physically supported primitives during lowering.

2. Retain repeated structure during lowering

Repeated arithmetic can remain compact during compilation. Store one loop body with iteration-dependent bindings \(\theta_i\) for widths, slices, and constants. With \(L\) iterations, the eventual operation is \[U=V_{L-1}(\theta_{L-1})\cdots V_0(\theta_0).\]

Inversion reverses the execution order

Reversing a repeated circuit requires undoing the last executed operation first. The table shows the order change explicitly.

Forward executionInverse execution
\(V_0,\ V_1,\ V_2\)\(V_2^\dagger,\ V_1^\dagger,\ V_0^\dagger\)

This saves the compiler from expanding identical structure too early. Each bound occurrence still executes in the emitted schedule. Reversing a loop reverses both its order and its enclosed operations, as the example shows.

3. Cache structure, remap local outcomes

A completed lowering can also be cached when the component type, parameters, chosen implementation, and work bindings match. Reusing its structure requires fresh measurement identities for the new occurrence, as shown below.

First occurrenceReplayed occurrence
Measure work \(\to m_1\); correct using \(m_1\)Measure work \(\to m_2\); correct using \(m_2\)

If the second occurrence reused the first readout in its correction, it would implement a different operation. Replay must also preserve ownership and factory-loan information, and invalidate entries when the context changes. The reused structure is scheduled separately at each occurrence.

4. Allocate states when timing is known

Factory assignments are deferred until timing is known. Lowering uses virtual resource qubits; scheduling consumes available states at injection and releases capacity after matching cleanup. The pool obeys \[A_{\ell+1}=A_\ell-I_\ell+C_\ell,\qquad0\le A_\ell\le R.\]

Here \(A_\ell\) is available capacity, \(I_\ell\) injections, \(C_\ell\) completed cleanups, and \(R\) the pool size. Preparation readiness and the single-injection limit must also hold. A CCZ use contains three ZZ couplings to data, and the final schedule assigns each use and cleanup to a physical factory.

5. Store the long schedule compactly

The emitted program is large, so layers use block-local Pauli bitmasks and flat instruction arrays. This makes compiler storage manageable without removing any of the measurements that the machine must execute.

6. Encode the placement insight explicitly

Placement plans capture the design insight explicitly. In the adder lane, bit \(i\) goes to block \(\lfloor i/7\rfloor\), slots \(3(i\bmod7)+\{0,1,2\}\), with slot 21 reserved for a relay. The compiler handles decomposition and timing within that plan, making the plan an essential part of the reproducible result.
summary: Lower large operations into supported measurements, retain repeated structure during compilation, and assign factories only when their timing is known.
title: Appendix D · How the hierarchy becomes a concrete schedule

body:
From a small LUT to the circuit IonQ uses

A classical table contains fixed words \(D_t\). The quantum task is to load the word selected by an unmeasured address: \(|j,y\rangle\mapsto|j,y\oplus D_j\rangle\). We will build that operation from a one-bit choice, extend it recursively, then follow the scheduling and cleanup used for IonQ's coordinate tables.

1. One nonlinear test controls an entire word

Let \(x\) select between words \(D_0,D_1\), with enable bit \(c\). Compute \(a=cx\), use it to XOR-load \(D_1\), then apply a CNOT from \(c\) to change it into \(c(1-x)\). This selects \(D_0\). The net output is \[y_{\rm out}=y\oplus cxD_1\oplus c(1-x)D_0=y\oplus cD_x.\] Restoring \(a=cx\) prepares the work bit for erasure.

Each word load uses CNOTs on its 1 positions. Thus one nonlinear AND serves the entire word. X-erasing that AND produces \((-1)^{\mu cx}\), canceled by conditional CZ. Wider words still need more output qubits, CNOTs, and communication, but no additional address test at this node.

2. Replace each word load with a smaller lookup

For two address bits \(x_1x_0\), split the table into its high-bit halves. Replace each constant-word box by a one-bit lookup controlled by the current selector. The same construction now applies \(y\mapsto y\oplus cD_{x_1x_0}\).

There are three ANDs: one for the split and one in each child. The circuit visits both children in a fixed order. On a basis branch, a zero selector disables a child's output contribution; the quantum computer does not measure the address to choose which gates to run.

3. An entire eight-entry LUT, with every box defined

Adding one more address bit joins two four-entry subtrees. The next circuit uses the already defined controlled lookup as its building block.

For address 101, the first half contributes nothing and the second chooses row 01, writing \(D_{101}\). In superposition, the same gates apply the corresponding word to each branch. Together the drawings specify an eight-entry lookup for arbitrary m-bit words.

The work bits hold prefix tests such as “the address begins with 10.” This is unary iteration: visit those tests in sequence and reuse their storage after each subtree. A depth-first traversal needs only \(O(k)\) prefix qubits for a k-bit address, rather than storing every row selector simultaneously.

\[C_0=0,\qquad C_k=1+2C_{k-1}=2^k-1,\qquad U_k=2C_{k-1}=2^k-2\quad(k\ge1).\]

The recurrence counts one AND per internal controlled node. Thus an uncontrolled eight-entry table uses six ANDs, and a 16-bit table uses \(U_{16}=65{,}534\). These are logical construction counts; placing and communicating the selectors adds the physical scheduling cost.

4. The paper: split 16 address bits into two controlled 15-bit traversals

For the paper's 16-bit address, separate a high bit \(h\) and 15 low bits \(\ell\). The two halves contain \(D^{(0)}_\ell\) and \(D^{(1)}_\ell\). Their controlled contributions combine as \[y\longmapsto y\oplus(1-h)D^{(0)}_\ell\oplus hD^{(1)}_\ell=y\oplus D_j.\] Since both are XOR updates, their order can be rearranged where resources permit.

The zipper construction in Ref. [68], §4.1 gives each half separate address copies and prefix work. One traversal prepares its next selector while the other writes to the common output. The three-bit drawing illustrates that alternation.

Writes sharing a target are still separated. The saving comes from overlapping private preparation work, at the cost of additional workspace. All table entries and their nonlinear tests remain in the computation. IonQ then evaluates this schedule with its own measurement timing model.

5. How IonQ distributes a selected row across code blocks

To distribute a selected row, the paper places traversal scratch and the lowest address bit in one memory block. Higher index bits are copied there when a CCZ needs them, then cleared. A relay carries the resulting selector to each output block so that block can apply its part of the word.

Zipper lookup adds a second set of index copies and a second relay in each target block. These copies share computational-basis information in an entangled state. The copy and fanout primitives provide their physical movement and measurement-based cleanup.

Yes: measurements replace coherent uncomputation

After a loaded word has been used, running the lookup backward would clear it coherently. Another option is to X-measure the temporary output, reset its qubits, and repair the induced phase on the retained address. Every outcome is accepted; no postselection is involved.

To follow the effect on an arbitrary computation, include a remaining register \(|\psi_j\rangle\) correlated with the address: \[|\Psi\rangle=\sum_j\alpha_j|j\rangle|F(j)\rangle|\psi_j\rangle,\qquad \sum_j|\alpha_j|^2=1.\] The cleanup must preserve these correlations as well as the address amplitudes.

For b measured bits, \(\langle m|H^{\otimes b}|F(j)\rangle=2^{-b/2}(-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}\). Orthogonal retained addresses make every outcome equally likely, \(\Pr(m)=2^{-b}\). Conditioning on that outcome leaves \[|\Psi_m\rangle=\sum_j\alpha_j(-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}|j\rangle|\psi_j\rangle.\]

The measurement reveals no address information, but it attaches a known sign to each branch. Apply \(D_m|j\rangle=(-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}|j\rangle\) to cancel it. Measuring \(F(j)\) in the computational basis would instead distinguish different table values and destroy those coherences.

Keeping the readout is essential. If it is discarded, averaging over the unknown signs removes coherence between addresses with different table words. Measurement, reset, and the recorded phase repair together implement the intended cleanup.

Measured temporary valueInduced phaseRequired correction
Copied bit a\((-1)^{\mu a}\)\(Z^\mu\) on a
AND ab\((-1)^{\mu ab}\)\(CZ^\mu\) on a,b
Lookup word F(j)\((-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}\)Generally nonlinear phase lookup on j

The table compares the repairs for three erased functions. Copies and ANDs need Clifford corrections. An arbitrary table word induces a general phase function of the address, whose implementation must be included in the resource count.

6. Free the loaded coordinates without measuring the address

For a coordinate word, X-readout gives \[\sum_j\alpha_j|j,F(j)\rangle\xrightarrow{M_X(B)=m}\sum_j\alpha_j(-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}|j\rangle.\] The same principle used for one AND now acts on many output bits, so the correction depends on their combined parity with the measured mask.

Once \(m\) is known, compute the classical one-bit table \(g_m(t)=m\cdot F(t)\pmod2\). A phase lookup of this table supplies exactly the sign needed to cancel the readout phase, as shown below.

Because the correction is diagonal in \(j\), operations preserving that address can continue while it is deferred. In point addition, the first and third coordinate lookups load the same words, so their masks combine. The full correction table is \[g(j)=(m_x^{(1)}\oplus m_x^{(3)})\cdot x_j\;\oplus\;(m_y^{(1)}\oplus m_y^{(3)})\cdot y_j\;\oplus\;m_{3x}^{(2)}\cdot (3x_j\bmod p).\]

These inner products use the coordinate bit strings, and the \(3x_j\) entry is reduced modulo the field prime before encoding. Algorithm 6 accumulates the masks and ends with LookupPhaseFix. Appendix E states that this compiled phase lookup does not use Ref. [22]'s phaseup optimization, so that additional saving is absent from the reported totals.

The construction follows the main paper's lookup discussion, Algorithm 6, and Appendix E, together with Ref. [68]'s recursive and zipper lookup. The diagrams expose the logical maps; the separately compiled placement determines their physical duration.

A copied address is an entangled control

An address can control operations in several places by sharing its computational-basis information. The resulting copies form one entangled state.

\[\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\longmapsto\alpha|00\rangle+\beta|11\rangle.\]

The final diagram shows how a copied address can also move. X-measuring a spare computational-basis copy gives a sign \((-1)^{m\cdot x}\), canceled by Z gates on the retained address. Erasing the original copy instead leaves the state at its destination.

These lookup and cleanup identities are independent of the hardware. Their measurement depth, communication cost, and ancilla allocation must be calculated for the architecture executing them.
